<!--
    SC 1.1.1 FAILURE (F30 — text alternative that is not an alternative: camera filename).
    This is a news article. The lead hero image is a photograph that DEPICTS a specific scene:
    a daytime street protest, a dense crowd marching past a domed city-hall building, people
    holding rectangular placards/banners aloft. The image is informative — it is the visual
    evidence for the story. Its alt attribute is alt="DSC_0481.JPG", the raw camera filename
    written by the DSLR. The alt is NON-EMPTY, so every ACT presence rule (23a2a8 "Image has
    non-empty accessible name") PASSES. But "DSC_0481.JPG" conveys NONE of the depicted content:
    a screen-reader user hears "D S C underscore 0 4 8 1 dot J P G, image" and learns nothing
    about a protest, a crowd, city hall, or banners.
    WHY AUTOMATED TOOLS MISS IT: axe/WAVE/Lighthouse only check that alt is present and
    non-empty; "DSC_0481.JPG" satisfies that. The ACT descriptive-name rule qt1vmo can only
    catch a name that misnames a DIFFERENT identifiable asset; "DSC_0481.JPG" names nothing
    identifiable, so qt1vmo cannot judge it wrong against the pixels. Deciding "this is a
    camera filename, not a description of a protest" requires reading the string AS a human
    and comparing it to what the photo actually shows — a meaning/intent judgment.
  -->

<!-- Informative hero photo: a daytime protest. Crowd marching past a domed city-hall
           building, raised rectangular banners. The alt is the raw DSLR filename. -->

    visually distinct item (a yellow rain jacket, a green hiking boot, a blue water bottle,
    an orange backpack). The images are informative — they are the only visual that tells a
    shopper what the product looks like. Each thumbnail's alt is the CMS image slug, e.g.

    Note the visible product TITLE below each card IS descriptive — but that title is a
    separate <a>/<h3>, not the image's accessible name, and the image-only link wrapping the
    thumbnail therefore exposes only the slug.
    WHY AUTOMATED TOOLS MISS IT: the alt attribute exists and is non-empty on every image, so
    axe/WAVE/Lighthouse pass. "prod-9921-thumb-2" names no identifiable brand asset, so the
    descriptive-name rule qt1vmo cannot judge it a wrong-identity. Deciding that a CMS slug is
    a programming reference and not a description of a yellow rain jacket requires reading the
    string as a human against the rendered pixels.
  -->

<!--
    SC 1.1.1 FAILURE (F30 / generic placeholder "photo").
    This is a company "Our team" staff directory. Each card shows a DISTINCT headshot — the
    illustrations differ by hair, skin tone, glasses, facial hair, so a sighted user can tell
    the four people apart visually. Every single headshot carries the identical generic
    placeholder alt="photo". The alt is NON-EMPTY (presence rules PASS) but "photo" tells a
    screen-reader user nothing: it neither identifies WHO is pictured nor describes anything.
    The name + title appear as adjacent text, but the image's own text alternative is the bare
    word "photo" repeated four times.
    Note: a portrait whose alt is just "photo" is still a 1.1.1 failure even though the
    person's name is in adjacent text, because the IMAGE'S text alternative does not serve the
    equivalent purpose — a blind user hears "photo, photo, photo, photo" while a sighted user
    sees four different faces.
    WHY AUTOMATED TOOLS MISS IT: "photo" is a non-empty alt, so axe/WAVE/Lighthouse pass.
    "photo" names no identifiable asset, so qt1vmo cannot flag an identity mismatch. Recognising
    "photo" as a generic placeholder rather than a description requires human meaning judgment.
  -->
<!-- Distinct face A: dark hair, glasses, beard -->
<!-- Distinct face B: light hair, no glasses -->
<!-- Distinct face C: curly hair, deeper skin tone -->
<!-- Distinct face D: short grey hair, smiling -->

    WHY AUTOMATED TOOLS MISS IT: alt is present and non-empty on all three, so axe/WAVE/
    Lighthouse pass. "Chart.jpg" names no identifiable asset, so qt1vmo finds no identity
    mismatch. F30 itself lists "Chart.jpg" verbatim as a non-alternative; catching it requires
    a human to read the filename and compare it to the data the chart actually shows.
  -->

<!--
    SC 1.1.1 FAILURE (F30 — CMS auto-derived alt from a WhatsApp-export filename).
    Long-tail, real WordPress behaviour: when no alt is typed, some themes/plugins fall back to
    the Media Library "title", which WordPress generates by stripping the extension and
    title-casing the filename. A photo shared via WhatsApp is named "IMG-20231104-WA0006.jpg",
    so the derived alt becomes "Img 20231104 Wa0006" — it LOOKS like words (capitalised tokens)
    rather than an obvious filename, which makes it sneakier than alt="image".
    The page is a Spanish-language recipe blog. The hero photo DEPICTS a specific dish: a bowl
    of red pozole with shredded chicken, radish slices, lime and a sprinkle of oregano. The
    alt "Img 20231104 Wa0006" is NON-EMPTY (presence rules PASS) and conveys none of the dish.
    WHY AUTOMATED TOOLS MISS IT: alt is present and non-empty, so axe/WAVE/Lighthouse pass. The
    string is title-cased and word-like, defeating naive "is-this-a-filename" heuristics, and it
    names no identifiable asset, so qt1vmo finds no identity mismatch. Recognising "Img 20231104
    Wa0006" as a title-cased WhatsApp filename (date 2023-11-04, WA0006) and NOT a description
    of pozole requires a human reading the string against the depicted dish.
  -->

<!-- Hero photo: a bowl of red pozole with shredded chicken, radish slices, lime wedge,
           sprinkle of oregano. Informative. Alt is the title-cased WhatsApp filename. -->

    Same KIND of informative photo as case-01 — a daytime street protest, a crowd marching past
    a domed city-hall building with raised banners — but here the alt is a genuine text
    alternative that serves the equivalent purpose:
      alt="Crowd marching past the domed City Hall building, holding banners reading 'Fair fares'"
    A screen-reader user gets the same essential information a sighted user gets: who/what is in
    the scene and what it conveys. This is the ONLY structural difference from the failing
    filename/placeholder cases — the depicted pixels are equally specific; the STRING is the
    variable. Including this control makes the aspect a meaning-of-the-string judgment, not a
    presence judgment.
    EXPECTED OUTCOME: passed. Presence rules pass (alt non-empty) AND the descriptive-name /
    equivalence check passes because the alt actually conveys the scene. Automated tools also
    "pass" this — but for the wrong reason (they only saw non-empty); the human-judgment layer
    agrees here, which is what distinguishes a true pass from the filename failures.
  -->

<!--
    SC 1.1.1 FAILURE — context/function-dependent equivalence (CONTROL-PURPOSE limb).
    The header of a public-library catalogue search. The search box's submit control is an
    <input type="image"> showing a magnifying-glass icon. Its alt is "magnifying glass" —
    a LITERALLY CORRECT description of the depicted icon. Because alt is non-empty, the
    control HAS an accessible name, so axe/WAVE pass it. But for non-text content that is a
    CONTROL, the name must describe the control's PURPOSE ("Search"), not what the picture
    looks like. The canonical G94 example is exactly this: "A search button uses an image of
    a magnifying glass. The text alternative is 'search' and not 'magnifying glass'."
    A correctly-labelled second submit (an arrow icon alt="Go") is included for contrast.
    WHY AUTOMATED TOOLS MISS IT: <input type="image"> with a non-empty alt has a valid
    accessible name, so "image input has alt" / "control has name" checks pass. No tool
    knows the control SUBMITS A SEARCH; recognising that "magnifying glass" names the icon
    rather than the action requires understanding the control's function.
  -->

<!-- DEFECTIVE CONTROL: image submit button whose alt names the ICON, not the action.
           It is a real search submit; its purpose is "Search" but it announces "magnifying glass". -->
<!-- CONTRAST CONTROL (correctly labelled): the second submit names its purpose. -->
<!-- DEFECTIVE AREAS: alt describes the SHAPE/COLOUR of the region, not the destination. -->
<!-- CONTRAST AREA (correctly labelled): alt names the destination. -->

    A boarding-pass detail screen in an airline web app. The action bar holds three icon

    an oddly SPECIFIC but LITERALLY CORRECT description of the depicted device (it even looks
    like a desktop inkjet). The control's purpose is "Print boarding pass", but its name
    describes the appliance in the picture. Because the alt is non-empty the button has a
    valid accessible name, so axe/WAVE pass it. The other two buttons are correctly
    purpose-named ("Add to Apple Wallet", "Email boarding pass") so a screen-reader user
    hears two real actions and one appliance ("inkjet printer, button").
    WHY AUTOMATED TOOLS MISS IT: the button's accessible name is non-empty, satisfying
    button-name. No tool knows the button triggers window.print(); recognising that "inkjet
    printer" names the device rather than the action ("Print boarding pass") needs human
    understanding of what the control does.
  -->
<!-- DEFECTIVE CONTROL: alt names the DEVICE in the icon, not the action this button performs. -->

<!--
    SC 1.1.1 FAILURE — context/function-dependent equivalence (CONTROL-PURPOSE limb).
    An order-confirmation screen in a food-delivery web app. While the kitchen hasn't
    started, the user can stop the order. The stop control is a red stop-sign (octagon)
    graphic implemented as an inline <svg role="img">; the SVG's <title> (its accessible
    name) is "Red octagon" — a LITERALLY CORRECT description of the depicted shape. The
    control's purpose is "Cancel order", but its name describes the geometry in the picture.
    Because the SVG has a non-empty accessible name AND the control is keyboard-operable,
    axe/WAVE see a named, focusable control and pass it. A second control next to it
    ("Track driver") is correctly purpose-named. A sighted user reads the stop sign as
    "cancel"; a screen-reader user hears "Red octagon, button" and cannot tell it cancels
    the order — and might fear pressing it.
    WHY AUTOMATED TOOLS MISS IT: the control has a non-empty accessible name (the SVG title),
    satisfying name checks. No tool knows the button cancels the order; recognising that
    "Red octagon" describes the shape rather than naming the cancel action needs human
    understanding of the metaphor and the control's function.
  -->

<!-- DEFECTIVE CONTROL: the stop-sign graphic's accessible name describes its SHAPE,
             not the action. This button cancels the order. -->
<!-- CONTRAST CONTROL (correctly purpose-named). -->
<!-- CONTROL-PURPOSE done right: the printer button is named for its ACTION. -->

<!-- LINK-PURPOSE done right: the globe image links to International Travel and its alt
           SERVES that purpose ("International Travel"), not the depiction ("globe"). -->

<!--
      The banner below is an IMAGE (inline-SVG data: URI). Its pixels contain the entire
      offer: the headline, the discount CODE "SAVE20", and the end date. The alt labels the
      image truthfully but DROPS every one of those words.
    -->

<!--
      Pull-quote IMAGE. Pixels contain the verbatim quotation AND attribution. The alt
      labels the image ("Decorative pull-quote graphic") but reproduces none of the words,
      and the surrounding prose never restates the quote.
    -->

<!--
    SC 1.1.1 FAILURE — inline SVG treated as a single image (role="img") whose accessible
    name omits the meaningful text drawn inside it (TT 7.A.1.d; F30 / G94 check #4).

    An internal recognition page shows an "Employee of the Quarter" certificate built as a
    decorative inline <svg role="img">. The SVG is named by a single <title> element:
    "Award badge". Because the SVG carries an explicit role="img" with that <title>, the
    accessibility tree collapses it into ONE image node named "Award badge" and the inner
    <text> elements — which spell out the actual award, the recipient, and the date —
    are NOT exposed. The visible pixels read:
        EMPLOYEE OF THE QUARTER
        Awarded to Dana Okafor
        Q2 2026 · Customer Success
    A sighted colleague reads exactly who won and when; a screen-reader user hears only
    "Award badge, image" and never learns the recipient is Dana Okafor.

    WHY AUTOMATED TOOLS MISS IT: ACT rule 7d6734 ("SVG element with explicit role has a
    non-empty accessible name") PASSES — the <title> gives a non-empty name. axe's
    "svg-img-alt" likewise passes. No checker reads the inner <text> glyphs, recognises
    they constitute the meaningful content, and verifies the name reproduces them. The
    <text> nodes are present in the DOM as drawing instructions but are suppressed from the
    a11y tree because the parent SVG is role="img" with its own name — so a tool that DID
    walk the DOM would still not treat them as the alternative. Confirming the name must
    contain the recipient/date is a manual transcription-equivalence judgment.
  -->

<!--
        Inline SVG with role="img" + a single <title>. The accessible name is the <title>
        ("Award badge"). The <text> elements below DRAW the real, load-bearing content
        (award name, recipient, quarter/team) but are not part of the accessible name and
        are suppressed because the SVG is a named image.
      -->

<!--
      The whole pricing comparison is ONE image. Pixels hold plan names, prices, seat
      counts, and event limits. The alt is a truthful label that reproduces none of it.
    -->

<!--
    SC 1.1.1 FAILURE — Arabic (RTL) sale banner image of text; the alt is a vague English
    summary that reproduces none of the Arabic offer words nor the promo code
    (TT 7.A.1.d; F30 / G94 check #4; also touches the Understanding "alternatives matching
    the language of content" note).

    A Gulf-region fashion store runs an Eid promotion. The campaign banner is a single
    flattened IMAGE (inline-SVG data: URI) whose pixels carry the whole offer in Arabic
    plus a Latin discount code:
        عروض العيد   (Eid offers)
        خصم 30% على كل الفساتين   (30% off all dresses)
        استخدم الرمز EID30   (use code EID30)
        حتى 15 شوال   (until 15 Shawwal)
    The author gave it alt="seasonal sale graphic" — non-empty, in ENGLISH, and a generic
    label. The Arabic shopper using a screen reader in Arabic hears an out-of-language
    English phrase that omits the discount, the category, the code EID30, and the deadline.
    Sighted shoppers get everything; AT users get "seasonal sale graphic".

    WHY AUTOMATED TOOLS MISS IT: image-alt passes (alt is non-empty). qt1vmo arguably
    passes (it labels the image as a seasonal sale graphic, which is true). No checker OCRs
    Arabic text out of a raster, recognises the embedded Latin promo code EID30, and
    verifies the alt reproduces those words in the page's language. Transcription
    equivalence ACROSS a script boundary is a manual judgment.
  -->

<!--
      Eid banner IMAGE. Pixels hold the Arabic offer text and the Latin code EID30. The alt
      is an unrelated-language generic label that drops all of it.
    -->

<!--
    SC 1.1.1 FAILURE — a scanned public-safety notice posted as an image; the alt is the
    one word "Public notice" and the safety-critical instructions/dates are lost
    (TT 7.A.1.d; F30 / G94 check #4).

    A municipal water-utility CMS page posts a "Boil Water Advisory". A records clerk
    scanned the signed paper notice and uploaded the resulting image rather than retyping
    it. The image (inline-SVG data: URI styled to look like a scanned form) contains the
    load-bearing, time-sensitive, life-safety content:
        BOIL WATER ADVISORY
        Affected: Maple Ward, zones 3 and 4
        Boil all tap water for 1 full minute before use
        In effect until: Thursday, June 25, 8:00 AM
        Questions: (555) 204-7781
    The alt is alt="Public notice" — non-empty and a fair label of the document type — but
    it drops the affected area, the boil duration, the lift date/time, and the hotline. A
    blind resident in Maple Ward learns only that "a public notice" exists, not that they
    must boil their water.

    WHY AUTOMATED TOOLS MISS IT: image-alt passes (alt present, non-empty); the name is a
    truthful document-type label so qt1vmo can pass too. No scanner OCRs the scanned notice
    to recover "boil for 1 minute" / "until June 25" and check the alt reproduces it.
    Judging that this image IS a block of safety text whose words must be transcribed is a
    manual visual/contextual call.
  -->

<!--
      Scanned advisory posted AS AN IMAGE. Pixels carry the affected area, the required
      boil time, the lift date/time, and the hotline. alt="Public notice" labels the
      document type but transcribes none of the safety-critical words.
    -->

<!--
    SC 1.1.1 PASS CONTROL — image of meaningful text whose alt DOES reproduce the same
    text (TT 7.A.1.d satisfied; G94 check #4 satisfied).

    This is the boundary case that sharpens the aspect: a yoga-studio promo banner that is
    ALSO a flattened image of text (inline-SVG data: URI), with the same kind of
    load-bearing offer copy as the failing cases — a class-pass discount, a promo code, and
    a deadline. The difference is ONLY in the alt: here the alt transcribes every displayed
    word, including the promo code and the date:
        Image pixels: "NEW STUDENT OFFER / 5 classes for $15 / Use code FLEX15 online /
                       Offer ends Friday, March 6"
        alt = "New student offer: 5 classes for $15. Use code FLEX15 online. Offer ends
               Friday, March 6."
    A screen-reader user receives the identical information a sighted user reads in the
    image — they CAN enter FLEX15 and know the deadline. Same component, same domain family
    of failure, opposite outcome — isolating that the defect is transcription-equivalence,
    not the mere presence of an image of text.

    WHY AUTOMATED TOOLS ALSO CAN'T CONFIRM THE PASS: the same OCR-and-compare step that
    automation can't do to FAIL the others is the step needed to CONFIRM this one passes.
    image-alt and qt1vmo pass here exactly as they do on case-01, yet only a human reading
    the image and the alt can tell that THIS alt actually reproduces the words (so it
    passes) while case-01's does not (so it fails). The boundary is invisible to scanners.
  -->

<!--
      Same kind of image-of-text as the failing cases (an inline-SVG promo banner with a
      code and a deadline), BUT the alt reproduces every displayed word verbatim, so a
      screen-reader user gets the same information as a sighted user. PASS.
    -->
<!-- The headline interest rate is presented ONLY by the background image on this paragraph. -->

/* THE DEFECT: the only place the headline rate is stated is inside this background image.
     180x52 SVG that renders the text "19.3% APR Typical Variable" as pixels. */

<!--
  SC 1.1.1 FAILURE (informative CSS background-image — F3 example 2 mechanism).
  Each row's STOCK STATUS (In stock / Last copy / Pre-order / Sold out) is conveyed ONLY
  by a CSS-class background-image sprite-glyph in the leading cell. The cell holds no text,
  no aria-label; the row's visible text is just artist/title/price/format. Two rows look
  identical to a screen-reader user even though one is "Sold out" and one is "In stock".
  Hide backgrounds / forced-colors mode -> all the glyphs vanish, taking the stock status
  with them, and that status is written nowhere as text.
  WHY AUTOMATED TOOLS MISS IT: the status carriers are <td> cells with class .st-* and a
  CSS background-image — no nameable element, so ACT 1.1.1 rules are Inapplicable and
  axe/WAVE/Lighthouse have nothing to flag. They cannot read the glyph pixels nor know
  that "Sold out" appears nowhere in the table.
-->
/* THE DEFECT: stock status lives only in these background-image glyphs, on text-empty cells. */

<!--
  SC 1.1.1 FAILURE (informative CSS background-image — required-field marker variant of F3,
  declared via the HTML style= attribute, the F3 "style attribute" carrier).
  Which fields are mandatory is shown ONLY by a small red-asterisk background image painted
  on a <span class="mark"> inside each required field's <label>, via an inline style= URL.
  There is no literal "*" character, no the word "required", and (deliberately) no
  required / aria-required attribute on the inputs — the obligation is purely a picture.
  Sighted users see red asterisks; AT users hear "First name, edit text" with no hint that
  it is mandatory. Hide backgrounds / forced-colors -> the asterisks disappear entirely.
  WHY AUTOMATED TOOLS MISS IT: the marker is a CSS background-image on a <span> — not a
  nameable image element — so ACT 1.1.1 rules are Inapplicable. Because there is no
  required/aria-required attribute, this is NOT the "field marked required" case a linter
  understands; nothing is technically "missing". Only a human looking at the rendered red
  asterisks can see that mandatory-ness is conveyed by image alone with no text equivalent.
-->
<!-- Phone is genuinely OPTIONAL: no marker. So the asterisk really does carry distinct info. -->

/* THE DEFECT carrier: each required label appends an empty <span class="mark"> whose ONLY
     content is a background-image red asterisk, set in the inline style= attribute (see HTML). */

<!--
  SC 1.1.1 FAILURE (informative CSS background-image — F3 example 3 carrier: background set
  dynamically by client script). Each dish's SPICE LEVEL is conveyed ONLY by chili-pepper
  glyphs that JavaScript paints as background images onto an empty <span class="heat">.
  The data lives in a data-heat="1|2|3" attribute that the script turns into a picture; the
  visible menu text gives only the dish name, description and price — never the words mild,
  medium or hot, and never any chili character. A diner who relies on a screen reader has no
  way to learn that the Phaal is the hottest dish on the menu. Disable JS, hide backgrounds,
  or use forced-colors mode and the heat indicator disappears with no text fallback.
  WHY AUTOMATED TOOLS MISS IT: the heat carrier is a script-set CSS background on a <span>
  with no role and no accessible name -> ACT 1.1.1 rules Inapplicable; axe/WAVE/Lighthouse
  run on the DOM and see only an empty <span>. A data-heat number is present, but no tool
  knows it encodes safety-relevant information that must also be available as text, nor can
  it OCR the rendered chili glyphs.
-->

/* THE DEFECT carrier: width grows with the number of glyphs the script paints; each glyph
     is a chili-pepper background image. No text equivalent of the heat level exists anywhere. */
